aAbout: Flightradar24 shows real-time aircraft positions built from ADS-B, MLAT, radar and FAA data fed by roughly 45,000 volunteer receivers, with airport departure and arrival boards, aircraft photos and deep flight history. Its consumer plans layer on features — up to 365 days of history, full aircraft details (age, serial, squawk, vertical speed), 15+ weather layers, aeronautical charts and oceanic tracks — and its iOS/Android apps, including 3D and cockpit views, are widely considered the best in flight tracking.
aStrengths: Flightradar24 is the deeper tool for watching the sky itself: a receiver network of roughly 45,000 feeders, up to 365 days of flight history, full aircraft details, 15+ live weather layers, ATC boundaries, aeronautical charts, oceanic tracks, CSV export and airport boards with live ETAs. Its apps are best-in-class for planespotting, and it reports more than 1,000,000 subscribers across its plans.
bAbout: Airplanes.live is a community-run ADS-B aggregator. Receivers built and hosted by enthusiasts pick up ADS-B and MLAT signals from the aircraft overhead, and the combined feed shows what is flying in your area right now — unfiltered and unobfuscated, including military aircraft, aircraft squawking an emergency and LADD-enrolled aircraft that other trackers suppress. The organisation was founded by four aviation enthusiasts and describes itself as not for profit, with by-laws that it cannot be sold, transferred or taken over by any one individual. The web map is free permanently with no accounts; a freemium iOS app adds a paid Pro tier.
bStrengths: Airplanes.live is the principled community choice: every aircraft its receivers hear is shown, unfiltered and unobfuscated — military jets, special-interest traffic and aircraft other trackers scrub. Feeders get the unfiltered MLAT results back, the web map is free permanently with no accounts, no ads and no trackers by its own account, and active feeders get the iOS app's Pro tier free. For planespotters and researchers who want the whole sky from a network run by enthusiasts rather than a company, it is the free, principled option.
betterAnswer: They solve different problems. Flightradar24 is the better everyday tracker: richer aircraft detail, up to 365 days of history, airport boards and polished apps for both phone platforms — filtered, and with the depth behind subscriptions. Airplanes.live is the better open window: a community-run, unfiltered ADS-B and MLAT map that is free on the web with no accounts, with a cheap Pro tier in its iOS app. If you want a tracker, open Flightradar24; if you want the unfiltered sky for free, open Airplanes.live.

intro: Flightradar24 and Airplanes.live track the same sky from opposite ends of the market. Flightradar24 (Sweden, founded 2006) is the polished mainstream tracker: real-time positions from a vast volunteer receiver network, rich aircraft detail, airport boards and best-in-class apps, with some traffic filtered and the depth sold by subscription. Airplanes.live is a community-run, not-for-profit ADS-B and MLAT aggregator founded by four aviation enthusiasts, built on the opposite promise — it will never filter or obfuscate aircraft data — with a web map that is free permanently and asks for no account at all.
pricingA: Free Basic tier with limited features. Paid consumer plans — Silver, Gold and Business — unlock 60+ premium features, with a 7-day free trial and pricing that varies by region (2026 reviews list Silver at roughly $12.99/year on annual billing). The Flightradar24 API is sold separately from the subscriptions.
pricingB: The web map is free — its app site says the unfiltered map is free, permanently — and no paid web plan is published. The iOS app is freemium: Free ($0) includes the full unfiltered live map, aircraft details, photos and routes, search, and no ads; Pro costs $2.99/month or $19.99/year in the app and adds live weather radar, ATC scope mode, advanced filters, an unlimited watchlist and push alerts. Pro is free for active feeders. Those Pro prices are iOS in-app prices, not web subscription prices.

seoDescription: Flightradar24 vs Airplanes.live compared: filtered polish, history and apps vs the free, community-run unfiltered ADS-B map — features, pricing and verdicts, plus a free third option.
seoTitle: Flightradar24 vs Airplanes.live (2026): Mainstream Tracker or Community Map?
verdictA: Choose Flightradar24 if you track for the love of it or for travel — planespotting, following aircraft globally, digging into history and aircraft detail, checking airport boards, or wanting polished apps on both iOS and Android with 3D views.
verdictB: Choose Airplanes.live if you want the whole sky for free — a community-run, unfiltered map with no accounts and no ads, military and emergency traffic included — and you're happy with a 2D web map and an iOS-only app for alerts and extras.
verdictLine: Flightradar24 is the polished product — filtered, app-first and subscription-deep. Airplanes.live is the community commons — unfiltered, free on the web and run by enthusiasts. Casual users and travellers will be happier in Flightradar24; enthusiasts who resent filtering will choose Airplanes.live.
worldEye: If you mainly want to glance at the sky rather than study it, WorldEye shows live flights free on a 3D globe — no signup — alongside live ships, satellites, weather, earthquakes, wildfires and 74,229 public cameras across 109 countries in the same view. WorldEye does not claim unfiltered military data like Airplanes.live or Flightradar24-grade flight history; it is the free, everything-at-once picture. An optional Pro tier ($7.99/week, $13.99/month or $74.99/year) adds the OSINT toolkit and intel feeds.
